paragraphs: A multilayer network records several kinds of relationships among the same entities. Its layers can share an underlying organization while differing in how particular nodes connect. This paper develops a latent space model that represents both kinds of structure, allowing information to be shared across layers without requiring identical connection patterns.

Each node receives a hidden vector shared across all layers, together with an effect specific to each layer. A separate connectivity matrix for each layer combines with these components to determine how edges form. The authors develop a projected gradient descent algorithm to estimate the model parameters efficiently.

The theoretical analysis explains a benefit of combining layers: under mild conditions, an upper bound on the estimation error for the shared latent structure decreases inversely with the number of layers. This is a conditional guarantee about an error bound. Simulations and two real data applications also demonstrate the proposed model’s superior performance in the studied settings.
icml-2020-a-flexible-latent-space-model-.tldr: A multilayer network model combines shared node representations with layer-specific effects, with estimation benefits from additional layers under mild conditions.

paragraphs: A reward-poisoning attacker changes the rewards a reinforcement learning agent receives so that it learns a policy chosen by the attacker. This paper studies how the permitted size of those changes affects whether an attack is possible. It establishes a lower threshold below which attacks are infeasible and a corresponding upper threshold above which attacks are feasible.

The paper then distinguishes attacks that depend only on the current transition from attacks that also respond to the agent’s learning process. That extra information matters because an adaptive attacker can change its interventions as learning progresses. The analysis therefore considers both the strength of reward manipulation and how intelligently it is timed.

Under mild conditions, adaptive attacks can induce the unwanted policy in a number of steps polynomial in the number of states, whereas non-adaptive attacks require exponentially many steps. A constructive Fast Adaptive Attack establishes the polynomial result. Experiments further show that deep reinforcement learning techniques can discover effective reward-poisoning attacks.
icml-2020-adaptive-reward-poisoning-atta.tldr: Reward-poisoning attacks can become exponentially faster when they adapt to an agent’s learning process, under the paper’s stated conditions.

paragraphs: Adversarial training uses deliberately perturbed examples to teach a model to withstand attacks. Searching for examples that maximize the model’s loss can make training conservative and sometimes hurt performance on ordinary inputs. This paper asks whether obtaining robustness necessarily requires that loss of natural generalization, and proposes friendly adversarial training as an alternative formulation.

The method still trains on adversarial examples that the current model confidently misclassifies. Within that set, however, it seeks examples with the smallest loss. This changes which errors become training material. The authors implement the idea by stopping an adversarial search procedure, such as projected gradient descent, early.

An upper bound on adversarial risk provides theoretical justification for the formulation. Empirically, the early-stopped search produces models that achieve adversarial robustness without compromising natural generalization in the reported experiments. These results support the possibility of avoiding the tradeoff through example selection; they do not establish that every model or task can avoid it.
icml-2020-attacks-which-do-not-kill-trai.tldr: Friendly adversarial training selects less extreme, confidently misclassified examples and empirically achieves robustness without sacrificing natural generalization.

paragraphs: This paper studies relationships among different event types in sequences where events occur at irregular times and depend on one another. Its target is Granger causality: the predictive relationships between event histories and subsequent events. Existing approaches face a tension between representing varied dependencies flexibly and making those learned dependencies understandable.

CAUSE separates the task into two stages. It first fits a neural point process to capture dependencies in the event sequence. It then applies an attribution method governed by explanatory axioms to extract a Granger causality statistic from the fitted process. The model learns the event relationships implicitly, and the attribution step turns that knowledge into an explicit statistic.

This design makes explanation part of the process for recovering relationships between event types. Across multiple datasets containing different forms of event dependence, CAUSE identifies inter-type Granger causality more successfully than a range of leading comparison methods. The reported finding concerns inference of these predictive relationships across the evaluated event sequences.
icml-2020-cause-learning-granger-causali.tldr: CAUSE combines neural event modeling with attribution methods to recover Granger causal relationships between event types.

paragraphs: Optimization becomes difficult when an objective is both nonconvex and nonsmooth: its landscape can have multiple competing regions and points where ordinary derivatives do not exist. This paper gives a finite-time analysis for finding stationary points in a broad class of such functions. The class retains a calculus chain rule and includes networks with ReLU and other nondifferentiable activations.

The authors first establish an obstacle: first-order methods cannot generally find an epsilon-stationary point in finite time for the studied problem. They therefore introduce a relaxed target called (delta, epsilon)-stationarity, allowing proximity within delta to an epsilon-stationary point. For smooth functions, the notion reduces to epsilon-stationarity.

The paper develops randomized first-order algorithms and bounds the work required to reach this relaxed target. A lower bound shows that the stochastic algorithm’s dependence on delta is optimal in the minimax sense. Experiments also show good performance when training ReLU networks, connecting the theoretical relaxation to a concrete nonsmooth learning problem.
icml-2020-complexity-of-finding-stationa.tldr: A relaxed stationarity criterion enables finite-time guarantees for nonsmooth, nonconvex optimization, with optimal dependence on its distance tolerance.

paragraphs: In multi-label classification, an example can have several correct labels. The F-measure balances finding those labels against avoiding incorrect predictions, but optimizing it directly is computationally difficult. This paper constructs convex substitute losses whose optimization is aligned with the F-measure in the limit of sufficient data.

The key observation is structural. Although the F-measure loss matrix for s labels has 2^s rows and columns, its rank is at most s^2 + 1. The authors use this low-rank property to build a family of calibrated surrogate losses. Their learning algorithms can be interpreted as solving s^2 + 1 binary probability estimation problems.

Calibration means that minimizing the surrogate risk yields a Bayes optimal classifier for the F-measure in the stated limiting setting. The paper also supplies a quantitative regret bound that transfers guarantees from the binary problems to the overall task. Experiments support the theory, connecting a tractable collection of probability estimates to the original evaluation objective.
icml-2020-convex-calibrated-surrogates-f.tldr: A low-rank property of the multi-label F-measure enables convex surrogate losses with calibration and regret-transfer guarantees.

paragraphs: LSTMs were introduced to help neural networks learn dependencies across long sequences, and their practical success makes the question of memory especially relevant. This paper asks whether RNNs and LSTMs possess long memory in a statistical sense. The distinction matters because success on sequence tasks and satisfying a formal definition of long memory are different claims.

The authors provide a partial answer by proving that RNNs and LSTMs lack long memory from the statistical perspective they study. They then introduce a definition of long-memory networks that requires model weights to decay at a polynomial rate. This turns the question into a structural requirement on how the model represents dependence over time.

To connect the theory with learning behavior, the paper makes minimal modifications that turn RNNs and LSTMs into long-memory networks. The modified models show superior performance in modeling long-term dependencies across various datasets. The contribution thus combines a formal diagnosis, a proposed architectural requirement, and empirical evidence that meeting it can improve the studied tasks.
icml-2020-do-rnn-and-lstm-have-long-memo.tldr: The paper finds that RNNs and LSTMs lack statistical long memory and proposes small modifications that improve long-term dependency modeling.

paragraphs: In a black-box adversarial attack, the attacker can submit inputs and observe feedback but cannot inspect the target model. Each query must therefore supply information useful for finding an input that fools the model. This paper focuses on query efficiency, identifying randomly sampled search directions as a source of wasted queries in previous approaches.

The authors formulate attack construction as an optimization problem with a limited query budget. Their analysis motivates learning along two paths: the sequence of adversarial examples and the sequence of directions used to search for them. Feedback from the target informs both how the candidate input changes and where the attack searches next.

The resulting dual-path distillation framework makes search direction selection responsive to knowledge already collected. Its importance lies in treating the search process itself as something to improve with feedback, alongside the adversarial example. Experiments suggest that this combined use of feedback can significantly improve query efficiency in the evaluated attacks.
icml-2020-dual-path-distillation-a-unifi.tldr: Dual-path distillation uses target-model feedback to refine both adversarial examples and search directions, improving query efficiency experimentally.

paragraphs: This paper analyzes when a graph neural network with one hidden layer can learn a model that generalizes. It considers regression and binary classification under a specific assumption: a ground-truth GNN with zero generalization error exists. Learning is then framed as recovering that model’s parameters from training data.

The proposed algorithm combines tensor initialization with accelerated gradient descent. The initialization supplies the starting point for the subsequent optimization, while the accelerated updates drive parameter learning. For regression, the authors prove convergence to the ground-truth model. For binary classification, they prove convergence to a model sufficiently close to it.

In both cases, the analysis establishes a linear convergence rate that is faster than ordinary gradient descent. The paper also investigates how the underlying graph affects the number of training examples required. Numerical experiments support the analysis and the algorithm’s effectiveness. These guarantees explain learning behavior within the assumed one-hidden-layer, ground-truth-model setting, with different recovery conclusions for the two prediction tasks.
icml-2020-fast-learning-of-graph-neural-.tldr: Under a ground-truth GNN assumption, tensor initialization and accelerated gradient descent provide fast recovery guarantees for one-hidden-layer networks.

paragraphs: GAN training must compare real data with a generated distribution that keeps changing. This paper attributes instability to the difficulty of matching features using mini-batch statistics while maintaining that balance. It proposes changing the discriminator’s representation so that real and generated samples are compared in a shared discrete feature space.

Feature quantization maps the samples’ features to values in an evolving dictionary. The dictionary reflects feature statistics from recent distribution history, providing a compact representation informed by more than the immediate comparison. According to the paper, this implicitly supports more robust feature matching as the generator changes during training.

The method can be added to existing GAN models with little extra training computation. Experiments cover three representative GAN models across ten benchmarks and show large improvements in FID scores over the corresponding baselines, reaching new state-of-the-art performance in the reported evaluation. The findings support modifying the discriminator’s feature representation as a practical way to improve GAN training and generated-image quality.
icml-2020-feature-quantization-improves-.tldr: Quantizing discriminator features into a shared, evolving dictionary improves GAN feature matching and substantially improves reported FID scores.

paragraphs: Off-policy reinforcement learning uses data collected under a distribution that can differ from the states visited by the policy being evaluated. GradientDICE estimates the density ratio between these distributions. That ratio describes their relative weighting and is the central estimation target of this paper.

The authors identify a conflict in the earlier GenDICE formulation. Ensuring positivity requires a nonlinear parameterization, even for consistency with a tabular representation. Yet introducing that nonlinearity destroys the convex-concave saddle-point structure that would support standard primal-dual convergence guarantees. Consequently, those optimization algorithms are not guaranteed to reach the desired solution.

GradientDICE changes the objective itself, drawing on the Perron-Frobenius theorem and removing the divergence used by GenDICE. This avoids the need for the problematic nonlinear parameterization. The authors prove convergence with linear function approximation. The contribution is therefore a reformulation that resolves the identified conflict and provides a convergence guarantee in a clearly specified representation setting.
icml-2020-gradientdice-rethinking-genera.tldr: GradientDICE reformulates off-policy density-ratio estimation to avoid a parameterization conflict and guarantees convergence with linear function approximation.

paragraphs: A prediction interval can have the correct coverage averaged over a dataset while remaining systematically overconfident or underconfident for particular groups. This paper studies a stronger requirement: calibration for individual samples in regression. The goal is to address errors that aggregate calibration can conceal and that can affect fairness or decisions made from predictions.

The authors show that individual calibration is possible in their regression setup if and only if predictions are randomized. In particular, the model outputs randomized credible intervals. Randomization removes systematic bias by exchanging it for variance, so the method changes the nature of prediction uncertainty rather than simply adjusting a fixed interval.

The paper designs a training objective that enforces this individual calibration requirement and uses it to learn randomized regression functions. The resulting models are better calibrated for arbitrarily selected subgroups. They can also provide higher decision-making utility against adversaries that exploit miscalibration, connecting the stronger calibration objective to consequences beyond average prediction coverage.
icml-2020-individual-calibration-with-ra.tldr: Randomized regression forecasts enable individual calibration and can improve subgroup calibration and decisions against adversaries exploiting miscalibration.

paragraphs: A reinforcement learning system may encounter new observation distributions when it moves between environments. This paper studies how to learn state abstractions that remain useful across those changes. A state abstraction gives the learner a representation of its observations, and the proposed approach connects that representation to features that are causal with respect to return.

For certain classes of environments, the authors prove that their method identifies an abstraction corresponding to the causal feature set with high probability. The guarantee therefore concerns both the information retained by the abstraction and the environments in which that identification succeeds. It provides a formal connection between identifying causal variables and constructing states for an MDP.

The paper also bounds model generalization error in the multi-environment setting. For nonlinear versions of the approach, experiments provide evidence of improved generalization over single-task and multi-task baselines. The theoretical identification result and the nonlinear empirical evidence together support causal state abstraction as a route toward transfer across observation distributions.
icml-2020-invariant-causal-prediction-fo.tldr: Causal state abstractions provide conditional identification guarantees and empirical improvements in reinforcement learning generalization across environments.

paragraphs: A useful hidden representation may need a particular structure: some factors should capture correlations, while others should preserve invariance. This paper presents a generative modeling framework for learning such structured latent factors from dependent, multivariate data. Its aim is to make desired relationships part of representation learning rather than leave the latent organization unspecified.

The framework expresses structural preferences through mask variables in a graphical model. These masks describe the dependency structure, and an extension of the multivariate information bottleneck provides a principled way to enforce it. The same framework also allows dependencies to be estimated automatically from data, giving flexibility in how much structure is supplied beforehand.

The resulting latent factors are intended to have meaningful interpretations tied to the chosen structural properties. The authors show that the framework brings many existing generative models under one formulation. They also describe applications to multimodal modeling, algorithmic fairness, and generalization outside the training distribution, illustrating the range of tasks where structured representations can matter.
icml-2020-learning-structured-latent-fac.tldr: A generative framework uses dependency masks and information bottleneck theory to learn latent factors with specified or data-estimated structure.

paragraphs: Learning from a stream becomes especially difficult when both the available measurements and their distribution change. In environmental monitoring, for example, old sensors can disappear and new ones can add features. This paper addresses that combined problem, where a model must cope with changes in what is observed as well as changes in the incoming data.

The authors introduce evolving discrepancy, a measure designed for comparisons involving both an evolving feature space and an evolving distribution. They use it to analyze generalization error. This gives the algorithm’s design a theoretical basis for handling the two forms of change together.

The resulting learning algorithm is implemented with deep neural networks. Synthetic experiments support the rationale behind the discrepancy measure, while extensive experiments on real tasks demonstrate the algorithm’s effectiveness. These two evaluations serve complementary purposes: one examines the proposed way of describing change, and the other tests the learning method motivated by that description.
icml-2020-learning-with-feature-and-dist.tldr: Evolving discrepancy supports generalization analysis and a neural learning algorithm for streams whose features and distributions both change.

paragraphs: Post-hoc calibration adjusts a trained classifier’s uncertainty estimates. This paper argues that a useful calibrator should preserve classification accuracy, work efficiently with limited data, and express a wide range of corrections. It finds that existing methods do not meet all three requirements together and proposes combining calibrators through ensembles and composition.

These Mix-n-Match strategies can improve off-the-shelf calibrators while provably maintaining the original classifier’s accuracy. Their purpose is to improve the uncertainty estimates without sacrificing the classifier’s predictive success. The authors report substantial gains in data efficiency and expressive power from these combinations.

The paper also examines how calibration is measured. Histogram-based expected calibration error can be misleading, especially with little evaluation data. The authors propose a kernel density estimator and prove asymptotic unbiasedness and consistency, properties describing its behavior as data increase. Across most experimental settings, their approaches outperform leading alternatives in both calibration and its evaluation, addressing two connected sources of uncertainty-estimation error.
icml-2020-mix-n-match-ensemble-and-compo.tldr: Mix-n-Match combines calibrators to improve uncertainty estimates while preserving accuracy, and introduces a better-supported calibration evaluation estimator.

paragraphs: Universal machine translation aims to translate between any pair of languages using shared representations. This paper studies when that ambition is theoretically possible. It establishes a lower bound showing that, without assumptions about language structure, algorithms learning shared sentence representations must incur large error on at least one translation task.

The positive result depends on additional structure: paired documents must arise from a natural encoder-decoder generative process. Under that assumption, a number of language pairs growing linearly with the number of languages can suffice to learn a good representation. This offers a theoretical basis for generalizing without observing the full quadratic collection of language pairs.

The arrangement of available pairs also matters. The paper analyzes connection graphs between languages and shows that longer paths lead to worse sample complexity. Its findings therefore identify both a barrier to unrestricted sharing and conditions that make sharing useful, while explaining why the pattern of multilingual training connections affects the amount of data needed.
icml-2020-on-learning-language-invariant.tldr: Shared translation representations face general impossibility results, but structured language generation allows learning from linearly many language pairs.

paragraphs: GAN-generated images offer potential for expanding small training datasets, but training the generator itself with little data remains a problem. This paper explores transferring knowledge from GANs already trained on large datasets. The source model can bring information that the limited target dataset does not contain on its own.

The authors investigate low-level filters close to the observations in both the generator and discriminator. Their natural-image experiments show that these filters can transfer to a target domain with a different perceptual appearance. Thus, useful reusable components can exist on both sides of the adversarial learning setup.

To adapt the transferred filters further, the paper introduces adaptive filter modulation, or AdaFM. This supplements filter reuse with a mechanism for adjusting the inherited components to the target domain. Extensive experiments demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed techniques for image generation with limited data. The findings support transferring and adapting pretrained GAN components as a practical approach to this training constraint.
icml-2020-on-leveraging-pretrained-gans-.tldr: Transferring low-level GAN filters and adapting them with AdaFM improves image generation in target domains with limited training data.

paragraphs: Unlabeled linear regression adds an unknown permutation to the usual regression problem: the correspondence between observations must also be recovered. This creates a computational burden, particularly in high dimensions. The paper proposes a one-step estimator and analyzes both its computational cost and the signal strength needed for permutation recovery.

For computation, the comparison is an oracle setting in which the regression coefficients are already known and only the permutation remains unknown. The proposed estimator has the same order of computational complexity as that easier reference problem. This is the basis for its computational optimality claim.

The statistical comparison is qualified by the stable rank of the regression coefficient matrix. When that rank is much smaller than log n divided by log log n, the required signal-to-noise ratio agrees with necessary recovery conditions up to the stated Ω(log log n) difference. The result therefore combines oracle-order computation with near-matching statistical requirements in a particular rank regime, rather than claiming an exact match in every setting.
icml-2020-optimal-estimator-for-unlabele.tldr: A one-step estimator matches oracle-order computation for unlabeled regression and approaches necessary recovery conditions in a specified stable-rank regime.

paragraphs: PEGASUS designs a self-supervised pretraining task specifically for abstractive summarization. It removes important sentences from a document and trains a large Transformer encoder-decoder to generate those sentences together from the remaining text. The missing sentences form a summary-like target, linking pretraining more directly to the later summarization task.

The model is pretrained on large text collections and evaluated on twelve downstream summarization tasks. These span news, science, stories, instructions, emails, patents, and legislative bills. This breadth addresses the paper’s concern that summarization pretraining should be tested systematically across varied domains.

The best PEGASUS model achieves state-of-the-art ROUGE results on all twelve evaluated datasets. In a low-resource setting, it exceeds previous leading results on six datasets using only 1,000 examples. Human evaluations also find summaries at human performance levels on multiple datasets. Together, these findings support the summary-oriented objective across both broad domain evaluation and limited-data adaptation, with the human-performance claim tied to the evaluated datasets.
icml-2020-pegasus-pre-training-with-extr.tldr: PEGASUS pretrains summarizers by reconstructing important missing sentences, achieving leading results across twelve summarization datasets.

paragraphs: Generative models commonly try to match a target distribution directly in the observed data space. This paper argues that training may be difficult when that space has far more dimensions than the data’s underlying structure. It proposes comparing generated and target distributions in the latent space of a standard autoencoder.

The encoder maps both distributions into that shared space, where the generator or decoder learns to match them. Reconstruction losses in both data and latent space enforce consistency, and the authors provide theoretical justification for those losses. The resulting perceptual generative autoencoder can use either maximum likelihood or a variational autoencoder objective.

With maximum likelihood, the approach extends reversible generative modeling to unrestricted neural architectures and arbitrary latent dimensionality. With the variational objective, it substantially improves sample quality over baseline VAEs. Among autoencoder-based generative models using simple priors, it reports state-of-the-art FID results on CIFAR-10 and CelebA. These findings connect latent-space matching to both modeling flexibility and measured generation quality.
icml-2020-perceptual-generative-autoenco.tldr: Perceptual generative autoencoders match distributions in encoded space, expanding architectural flexibility and improving reported sample quality.

paragraphs: Learning a Markov random field can mean identifying which variables are connected or also estimating the parameters on those connections. This paper studies both goals under differential privacy, including models such as the Ising model. Its central question is how privacy changes the difficulty of recovering a model’s structure versus its numerical parameters.

The authors provide algorithms and lower bounds for pure, concentrated, and approximate differential privacy. Without privacy, structure learning and parameter learning have roughly comparable complexity. Under privacy, their dimensional dependence separates sharply: only structure learning with approximate differential privacy retains the logarithmic dependence available without privacy.

Changing either that learning goal or that privacy notion requires polynomial dependence on dimensionality in the studied setting. The distinction matters especially for high-dimensional data, where logarithmic and polynomial growth lead to very different scaling. By combining achievable algorithms with lower bounds, the paper shows that the separation reflects a fundamental privacy cost rather than merely a weakness of a particular algorithm.
icml-2020-privately-learning-markov-rand.tldr: Differential privacy sharply separates structure and parameter learning for Markov random fields, with favorable dimensional scaling only in one studied setting.

paragraphs: Actor-critic reinforcement learning combines a policy-learning component with a critic that estimates value. This paper addresses the off-policy setting with function approximation, where learning uses data associated with a different policy. It introduces COF-PAC, presented as the first provably convergent two-timescale actor-critic algorithm for this setting.

The central addition is an emphasis critic alongside the conventional value-function critic. This extra critic is trained using Gradient Emphasis Learning, or GEM, which combines key ideas from Gradient Temporal Difference Learning and Emphatic Temporal Difference Learning. The convergence argument depends on using both critics within the proposed algorithm.

The guarantee allows a nonlinear actor while requiring linear critics. That distinction is an important part of what the result establishes: flexibility in the policy representation is compatible with convergence in the stated critic setting. The paper’s contribution is a specific algorithm and supporting convergence analysis, showing how the added emphasis-learning component enables a theoretical guarantee for the complete actor-critic procedure.
icml-2020-provably-convergent-two-timesc.tldr: COF-PAC adds an emphasis critic to obtain a convergence guarantee for two-timescale off-policy actor-critic learning with linear critics and a potentially nonlinear actor.

paragraphs: Finding equilibria in large sequential zero-sum games with hidden information can be formulated as a linear program. However, the memory demands of standard linear programming formulations have made them difficult to scale. This paper revisits that approach by changing how the game’s payoff information is represented.

The authors develop a practical algorithm that factors a large payoff matrix into two matrices that are typically much sparser. Using this factorization, they express the equilibrium problem as a linear program whose size is only a logarithmic factor larger than the representation used by counterfactual regret minimization. This makes modern linear program solvers usable on games previously constrained by memory.

Experiments on poker endgames show performance competitive with modern, game-specific counterfactual regret minimization methods, with improvements often reaching orders of magnitude. The linear programming approach can also compute exact solutions, unlike the iterative comparison methods discussed in the paper. The contribution shows how a sparser formulation can make an established optimization tool competitive for large game-solving problems.
icml-2020-sparsified-linear-programming-.tldr: Sparse payoff-matrix factorization makes linear programming competitive for large zero-sum game equilibria and enables exact solutions.

paragraphs: Stochastic particle-optimization sampling represents a Bayesian sampling approach that brings together stochastic gradient MCMC and Stein variational gradient descent. It already has finite-time convergence theory and can avoid the particle-collapse problem associated with SVGD. This paper studies how reducing stochastic variance can further improve that sampling framework.

The authors introduce three variants: SAGA-POS, SVRG-POS, and SVRG-POS+. The last variant avoids full gradient computations. For each method, they provide non-asymptotic convergence guarantees measured with the 2-Wasserstein metric and analyze computational complexity. These results describe progress after finite computation rather than only behavior after an unlimited run.

The analysis yields better convergence rates than existing variance-reduced stochastic Langevin methods, with a stated cost: the particle-based algorithms need more storage during training. Experiments on synthetic and real datasets align with the theoretical findings. The paper therefore identifies a concrete convergence-versus-memory tradeoff while establishing variance reduction as a useful extension of stochastic particle sampling.
icml-2020-variance-reduction-in-stochast.tldr: Three variance-reduced particle samplers improve theoretical convergence rates over compared Langevin methods while requiring more storage.
